# Local resolution weighted composite of Martigny

This tutorial runs the whole pipeline, from search to composites, for a small
area around Martigny in the Swiss canton of Valais. The town lies on the flat
floor of the Rhône valley, where the river bends to the north, between steep
slopes that face in many directions. It compares a composite of the ascending
orbits, one of the descending orbits, and one that combines both with local
resolution weighting (LRW).

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

from dotenv import load_dotenv

root = next(p for p in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents) if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists())
load_dotenv(root / ".env")
(root / "cache/docs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
os.chdir(root / "cache/docs")
```

## Find the grid squares and their bursts

The area is a box of about 7 by 9 km around the town. It touches four 10 km
squares of the MGRS grid, all in UTM zone 32 North. The composites cover these
squares whole, so the search covers them too, through the union of their
bounding boxes, as in
[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#set-up). It returns every
VV burst of August 2025 that overlaps them:

```{python}
import shapely
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import (
    BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter,
    RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange,
)

fm = FileManager("data/martigny")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20))
print(", ".join(square.mgrs_code for square in squares), {str(square.crs) for square in squares})

search_area = shapely.union_all([box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox) for square in squares])
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV"))

bursts.df.groupby(["pass_direction", "rel_orbit_number"]).agg(
    acquisitions=("date", lambda dates: dates.dt.date.nunique()),
    bursts=("burst_id", "size"),
    sub_swaths=("sub_swath", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.unique()))),
    satellites=("parent_product_name", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.str[:3].unique()))),
)
```

Three relative orbits cover the squares: orbit 88 on ascending passes, in the
evening, and orbits 66 and 139 on descending passes, in the morning. Each
orbit was imaged five times in August, by Sentinel-1A and Sentinel-1C in turn.
Orbit 88 needs two bursts per acquisition to cover the squares, orbit 66
three, and orbit 139 five, from two neighboring sub-swaths, which makes 50
bursts in total. The descending orbits contribute twice as many acquisitions
as the ascending one.

## Process the bursts

Since the squares share one zone, all 50 bursts are processed in one batch, in
that zone, at the 20 m pixel size of the composites. This follows the
[AOI-first order](area-to-composites.qmd#aoi-first):

```{python}
#| output: false
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=squares[0].crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20),
).raise_on_failure().products
```

## Compose every square

Each square is composed from the products whose bursts reach it, twice: once
per pass direction with `compose_rtc_by_pass()`, and once across both
directions with `compose_rtc_lrw()`, which also writes the quality layers.

```{python}
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
lrw, by_pass = [], []
for square in squares:
    footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
    square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
    lrw.append(weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window))
    by_pass.append(weighter.compose_rtc_by_pass(square_rtc, square, time_range=window))
    print(f"{square.mgrs_code}: {len(square_rtc)} bursts")
```

## Compare the viewing directions

Sentinel-1 looks to the right of its track. On ascending passes it flies
roughly north and looks east, so slopes facing west are turned toward it;
on descending passes it flies south and looks west, toward slopes facing
east. A slope turned toward the radar is squeezed into few pixels and seen
coarsely, and one turned away is stretched over many pixels and seen finely,
unless it is so steep that the radar cannot see it at all. Such a slope lies
in radar shadow, and the products of that direction have no value there.

The figure joins the four squares of each composite into one mosaic and shows
the area of interest. Red marks the pixels without a value, which a pass
composite has where its direction sees only radar shadow. The rectangles mark
three sample areas: the valley floor east of the town (white), a slope facing
north-west (magenta) and one facing north-east (cyan).

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Backscatter composites of August 2025 around Martigny: the five ascending acquisitions (left), the ten descending acquisitions (middle), and all fifteen combined with local resolution weighting (right). Red marks radar shadow, where a composite has no value."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from rasterio.merge import merge
from rasterio.transform import rowcol
from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds
from s1bursts.product import Layer


def mosaic(composites, layer=Layer.MEASUREMENT):
    """Join the squares of one layer; return the data and its transform."""
    data, transform = merge([fm.get_product_path(c, layer) for c in composites])
    return data[0].astype("float32"), transform


def km_extent(data, transform):
    """Return the extent of a mosaic in kilometers, for imshow."""
    rows, cols = data.shape
    left, top = transform.c, transform.f
    return [v / 1000 for v in (left, left + transform.a * cols, top + transform.e * rows, top)]


crs = squares[0].crs
composites = {
    "Ascending": mosaic([c["Ascending"] for c in by_pass]),
    "Descending": mosaic([c["Descending"] for c in by_pass]),
    "LRW": mosaic(lrw),
}
areas = {
    "valley floor": (box(7.100, 46.110, 7.115, 46.120), "white"),
    "slope facing north-west": (box(7.031, 46.115, 7.038, 46.119), "magenta"),
    "slope facing north-east": (box(7.043, 46.110, 7.050, 46.114), "cyan"),
}
view = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *aoi.bounds)
viridis = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
viridis.set_bad("tab:red")  # pixels without a value: radar shadow

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.6), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (name, (data, transform)) in zip(axes, composites.items()):
    image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(data), extent=km_extent(data, transform),
                      cmap=viridis, vmin=-15, vmax=0)
    for area, color in areas.values():
        x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *area.bounds)
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0 / 1000, y0 / 1000), (x1 - x0) / 1000,
                                   (y1 - y0) / 1000, fill=False, edgecolor=color, linewidth=1.5))
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=(view[0] / 1000, view[2] / 1000),
           ylim=(view[1] / 1000, view[3] / 1000))
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Gamma-0 (dB)")
plt.show()
```

The median of each composite in the three sample areas puts numbers on the
comparison. The medians are taken in linear units and converted to decibels
afterwards, and they skip the pixels without a value:

```{python}
def median_in(data, transform, area):
    """Median of a mosaic within a lon/lat rectangle."""
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *area.bounds)
    (top, bottom), (left, right) = rowcol(transform, [x0, x1], [y1, y0])
    return np.nanmedian(data[top:bottom, left:right])


pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        area_name: 10 * np.log10(median_in(data, transform, area))
        for area_name, (area, _) in areas.items()
    }
    for name, (data, transform) in composites.items()
}).round(1)
```

How much of each area a composite misses in shadow:

```{python}
def share_missing(data, transform, area):
    """Share of a mosaic's pixels without a value within a lon/lat rectangle."""
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *area.bounds)
    (top, bottom), (left, right) = rowcol(transform, [x0, x1], [y1, y0])
    return np.isnan(data[top:bottom, left:right]).mean()


pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        area_name: f"{share_missing(data, transform, area):.1%}"
        for area_name, (area, _) in areas.items()
    }
    for name, (data, transform) in composites.items()
})
```

On the valley floor the three composites look alike: the fields, the town and
the river show the same pattern in each. The ascending composite is 0.8 dB
brighter there than the descending one, an offset that is close to uniform
across the floor and comes from the different times of day and incidence
angles of the two directions rather than from the terrain. The LRW composite
lies between the two.

On the slopes, the difference between the directions changes with the way
the slope faces. Each direction smears the slopes turned toward it into
coarse streaks and reads them brighter, and it loses the steepest slopes
turned away from it to shadow. The slope facing north-west is 2.5 dB brighter
in the ascending composite than in the descending one, which has no value on
22.4 % of it. The slope facing north-east is 1.5 dB brighter in the descending
composite, and the ascending one has no value on 13.5 % of it.

The LRW composite has a value everywhere: where one direction sees only
shadow, it takes the pixel from the other. Elsewhere it leans toward the
direction that sees each slope from behind. On the north-west slope it is
within 0.4 dB of the descending composite. On the north-east slope it lies
about midway, although the descending orbits supply two thirds of the
acquisitions; their squeezed view of that slope gets less weight. Across the
map, the LRW composite keeps the sharper view of each slope.

## Read the quality layers

The LRW composite comes with two quality layers. The figure shows them for
the four squares, with the composite for reference:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The LRW composite of the four grid squares (left), the number of acquisitions that contributed to each pixel, QA-NUM (middle), and the composite quality, QA-CQM, in decibels (right)."
layers = {
    "LRW composite (dB)": (Layer.MEASUREMENT, dict(cmap="viridis", vmin=-15, vmax=0)),
    "QA-NUM": (Layer.QA_NUM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=15)),
    "QA-CQM (dB)": (Layer.QA_CQM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=-8, vmax=8)),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 4), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (title, (layer, style)) in zip(axes, layers.items()):
    data, transform = mosaic(lrw, layer)
    if layer != Layer.QA_NUM:
        data = 10 * np.log10(data)
    fig.colorbar(ax.imshow(data, extent=km_extent(data, transform), **style), ax=ax,
                 orientation="horizontal")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (km)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
num, _ = mosaic(lrw, Layer.QA_NUM)
cqm, transform = mosaic(lrw, Layer.QA_CQM)
floor, _ = areas["valley floor"]
shares = pd.Series(num.ravel()).value_counts(normalize=True)
print("Share of pixels by QA-NUM:", {n: f"{shares.get(n, 0):.1%}" for n in (15, 10, 5)})
print(f"QA-CQM on the valley floor: {median_in(cqm, transform, floor):.2f}")
```

`QA-NUM` counts the acquisitions that carry weight in each pixel. All fifteen
contribute almost everywhere, on 94 % of the four squares and on the whole
valley floor. The exceptions are the steepest slopes, where one direction
looks into radar shadow and its acquisitions get no weight. Ten acquisitions
remain where one orbit drops out, on 3.4 % of the squares: the ascending one
on slopes facing east, or one of the descending ones on slopes facing west.
On a few very steep slopes facing west, 0.7 % of the squares, both descending
orbits see shadow and only the five ascending acquisitions remain.

`QA-CQM` rates the combined resolution of each pixel. It is nearly constant
on the valley floor, about 0.83 (−0.8 dB), since flat ground is seen alike from every
orbit. It is highest on the slopes facing west, which the ten descending
acquisitions see from behind and in fine detail, and lowest on the steepest
slopes, which every acquisition sees squeezed or not at all. A pixel with a
low `QA-CQM` is reported at the same 20 m as the others but describes the
ground more coarsely; [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd)
explains both layers.
